GBR.mechanism: A complaint that is received and then weighed against the standing of the man it names, and institutions that end the problem by sending the man to another country.
GBR.story:
A pupil in Rochdale went to the police in 1968 about Cyril Smith, who had helped set up a hostel for boys in the town, and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 the Director of Public Prosecutions, the official who decides whether the state brings a criminal charge, advised against prosecuting, and Smith was given an assurance that he would not be. He became the town's Liberal MP two years later and was knighted in 1988, after Margaret Thatcher had been told. Eight men said he had indecently assaulted them as teenagers. He died in 2010 never charged, and in 2012 prosecutors said he should have been. The national inquiry for England and Wales found no evidence that anyone pressured the DPP, but it did find "considerable deference to power" in the discussions before the knighthood. Deference of that kind needs no instruction and leaves no document.

Complaints about the BBC presenter Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958, and two investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. After an ITV documentary a year after his death, the Metropolitan Police and the NSPCC recorded 214 crimes across 28 police force areas from 1955 to 2009, reported by 450 people. The same report found no clear evidence of a paedophile ring, which is the point: he did not need one. He abused children in the hospitals and studios he was invited into, and his fame made each separate complaint look unpromising to whoever received it.

Institutions had another way to end a problem: move the man. In 1982 an internal report for the Iwerne Trust, which ran evangelical summer camps for boys, described the beatings given by its chairman, John Smyth QC. Nobody told the police, who heard only in 2013, and the 2024 Makin review found an "active cover-up" and called Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa". He left for Zimbabwe in 1984 and founded camps of his own for boys there in 1986, and nobody warned the Zimbabwean authorities. A job reference does the same work in smaller print: Fettes College in Edinburgh dismissed the teacher Iain Wares in 1979 and gave him a glowing testimonial, which is what the next employer reads instead of the reason he left. He went on to abuse children in South Africa.

Two loud British allegations failed on examination. An inquiry found no evidence that MI5 used Belfast's Kincora boys' home for blackmail, and the Westminster "VIP ring" was invented by Carl Beech, who was jailed.

Britain's record is not mainly a story of abuse nobody reported. The reports were made, often decades early, and what varied was the standing of the accused and the nerve of the person who took the complaint. When a British case next surfaces, find the year of the first report and who received it, then ask what that person had to lose by acting on it.

IND.mechanism: A state that pays private charities to hold children and then does not look inside, so abuse becomes visible only when an outsider audits or a child runs, and whether the case goes anywhere depends on the local standing of the accused.
IND.story:
Bihar's social welfare department asked a university to check on the homes it was paying for. In April 2018 the Koshish unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences handed back an audit of 110 children's homes across 38 districts, grading each as better run, administratively negligent or criminally negligent. The team's task was to go in and look, which was more than the department had been doing. At one home in Bhagalpur the staff would not produce the key to the complaint box and said it was lost, which closes the only private channel a child in care has. The audit graded a girls' home in Muzaffarpur, run by a state-funded charity under Brajesh Thakur, as criminally negligent. A police report, the document that formally opens a criminal case in India, was filed on 31 May 2018, and medical examinations indicated sexual abuse of 34 girls, most of them children. The district child protection officer was among the accused and the state welfare minister resigned. The Supreme Court moved the trial out of Bihar to Delhi because the accused were influential locally — an admission that where a case is heard decides whether witnesses and police stay reliable. Thakur and 18 others were convicted in January 2020.

Influence is plainer when the accused holds office. A girl in Unnao district accused Kuldeep Singh Sengar, then a state legislator for the governing BJP, of raping her in 2017. Her father died in police custody, and Sengar was arrested only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it. He was convicted in December 2019 and sentenced to life.

Other cases open by accident. In Deoria, Uttar Pradesh, a ten-year-old girl escaped to a women's police station in 2018 and said girls were driven away in the afternoons and brought back crying in the morning; police rescued 24 girls. The state had withdrawn that charity's recognition and funding a year earlier and the home had carried on, because taking a home off a list is not the same as sending someone to close it.

In adoption the pull was money. A chargesheet said a Hyderabad home had earned Rs 3.33 crore from intercountry adoptions in 1999-2001; ten people, among them a nun, were sentenced in 2005 to six months for cheating and forgery, the paperwork offences rather than the sale of a child. India sent 12,511 children abroad between 2003 and 2022.

India has held no national inquiry into institutional abuse, and South Asia has no representative survey of online abuse, so this record is largely what one university audit and one child's escape happened to produce. Scholars note that allegations here "often remain informal and rarely progress to formal charges". When you read an Indian case, ask who last inspected the home and whether anyone could open the complaint box.

ESP.mechanism: A country where the abuse was state policy and the reckoning has turned on two technical things: a legal clock that ran out before victims could use it, and who was willing to turn percentages into a count.
ESP.story:
After the civil war ended in 1939, about 30,000 children were placed in state care in Spain. A 2008 ruling by the judge Baltasar Garzón described most of them as "war orphans with parents who were dead, imprisoned, exiled, in hiding, or disappeared". Their names were changed so they could be handed to families loyal to the Franco regime, which is what makes a child untraceable: with a new name and a new birth record there is nothing for a mother to follow. Girls in homes run by the Women's Protection Board were pressured into giving up babies. Two things protected the system afterwards: a 1977 amnesty law barring prosecution for acts of that period, and the disappearance of many of the board's files in 1996.

The first trial came in 2018. A Madrid court found the retired gynaecologist Eduardo Vela, then 85, responsible for taking a newborn, faking a birth and falsifying official documents in 1969 — and acquitted him, because the statute of limitations had run. That is the deadline after which a crime can no longer be prosecuted, counted here from the moment the child reached adulthood in 1987. The clock ran out while she still held the forged certificate and had no reason to doubt it.

Counting is the other fight. In 2011 the families of 261 babies who vanished from hospitals asked the attorney general to investigate doctors and nurses, and lawyers put the number taken as high as 300,000. In 2026 forensic geneticists at Spain's national institute of toxicology and forensic sciences found no evidence of systematic theft from hospitals and called that figure a hoax, while not disputing the coercion inside Francoist institutions or the 30,000 children in state care. The first official inquiry into abuse in the Catholic Church was more careful. The Ombudsman, a public official who can investigate the state, commissioned a survey of 8,013 adults: 11.7% said they had been abused before 18, 1.13% in a religious setting, 0.6% by a priest or religious. He published the percentages and declined to multiply them across the population. Newspapers did, arriving at about 440,000, and the bishops apologised while disputing it.

Spain is also an offender's home country. Morocco sentenced the retired Spanish professor Daniel Galván in 2011 to 30 years for raping 11 children aged 4 to 14, and in 2013 the king pardoned him among 48 Spanish prisoners, a favour between governments. It was revoked after protests in Rabat, by which time he had left on an expired passport.

Spain shows that a case can be proved in open court and still end in acquittal, because the deadline was counted from a date the victim knew nothing about. It also shows a number inflating past its evidence, at a cost to the survivors whose own claims were sound. When you meet a Spanish figure, ask who produced it and whether they multiplied out a survey; when a case fails, ask when the clock was set running.

COD.mechanism: The people sent to protect and feed children used the power that gave them to obtain sex, and the organisation that sent them has no power to punish anyone, because discipline belongs to the soldier's or the employee's own government.
COD.story:
In the spring of 2004, Congolese women and local media said that UN soldiers stationed at Bunia, in the east, were having sex with girls in the town. The UN's internal investigators spent May to September there and reported that it happened "with regularity", usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many of the girls were under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations made to the mission, most could not be investigated because they were not specific enough: a girl who knows a nickname, a uniform and a nationality has not given investigators anyone to question. Six were fully substantiated.

Substantiated is not the same as punished. Soldiers lent to a UN mission stay under the criminal law of the country that sent them, so the UN can send a man home and do nothing more. The Secretary-General's 2025 report shows how few such cases finish: one Togolese officer was repatriated and imprisoned for 60 days, while others are marked "pending additional information from the member state", meaning the UN asked a government a question and has had no answer.

The same arrangement of power reappeared without soldiers. During the Ebola response in North Kivu and Ituri from 2018 to 2020, an independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of them established with certainty as employees of the World Health Organization. Most were Congolese staff hired for the response who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for a job. Where the response is the main source of paid work, the man who decides who is hired does not need force. The youngest person the commission heard was a girl of 13 selling phone cards in Mangina, who said a WHO driver raped her. Nine rape allegations were recorded and 29 women and girls became pregnant.

Armed groups take children outright, and a court reaches only what prosecutors charge. The International Criminal Court's first conviction, in 2012, was of Thomas Lubanga for using children under 15 as soldiers in Ituri; sexual violence against the girls among them was raised at trial but never charged, so it forms no part of his conviction. In 2019 the court convicted Bosco Ntaganda of rape and sexual slavery as well. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls, 47 of those cases by Congo's own army, and the abduction of 815 children.

Congo shows that an allegation, an investigation and a finding can all be completed without anyone standing trial, because the power to prosecute sits with a government thousands of miles from the child. When a mission or an agency publishes its allegation numbers, ask how many ended in a court, and in whose court.

NGA.mechanism: Three separate trades in the same country — children taken from schools as a tactic of war, babies produced to order for sale, and girls moved abroad on a debt and an oath — and a record that only ever counts the children who came back.
NGA.story:
On the night of 14 April 2014, gunmen from Boko Haram drove into Chibok, in Borno state, emptied the dormitories of the girls' secondary school and loaded 276 pupils onto trucks. More than 50 got away within hours by jumping off the lorries. Ten years later Amnesty International said 82 of the girls were still held and that 20 of those released had been forced to marry former fighters. Taking schoolchildren works as a tactic because it is cheap and hard to reverse: the captives are dispersed, and a government that wants them back has to negotiate. Schools were raided again at Dapchi in 2018, where 110 girls were taken, and at Kankara in 2020, where more than 300 boys were. In 2024 alone the UN verified the abduction of 991 children in Nigeria and sexual violence, all of it forced marriage, against 419.

A separate trade runs through buildings registered as clinics and orphanages, which Nigerian police call baby farms. In 2011 police in Aba freed 32 pregnant girls, most aged 15 to 17, held so their babies could be sold; four already sold were recovered. In 2018 Lagos officials said 162 children had been taken out of a "baby factory" and two unregistered orphanages. The business works because a baby with no birth record can be given any history, and adoption abroad from Nigeria is still open: 3,263 children went out between 2003 and 2022.

Girls are moved out of the country on two instruments that need no violence. The 2025 US trafficking report describes organised groups, some tied to Nigerian cult confraternities, placing women and girls in prostitution in Italy, Spain and the UK, and moving others to gold-mining regions of Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. Most come from Edo State and travel overland through Niger and Libya. The journey is treated as a loan set at a figure she cannot clear, so she works until the lender says the debt is paid, and an oath sworn before departure makes leaving a spiritual danger too. The UN's migration agency recorded an almost 600 per cent rise in likely victims arriving in Italy by sea between 2014 and 2017.

Online the direction reverses: two brothers in Lagos used hacked Instagram accounts to pose as a girl, obtained explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded $1,000. He died by suicide in March 2022, and they were extradited and sentenced to 17 and a half years each.

Almost every Nigerian figure here comes from a raid or a release, so it counts children who were found rather than children who were taken, and West and Central Africa has no representative survey of online abuse to put behind those counts. When you read that a number of children were rescued, ask how many were taken, and who is still counting the ones who have not come back.

ITA.mechanism: A country whose church is not required to tell the police, and which therefore has no record of its own: almost everything known about Italian cases was established in other countries' courts.
ITA.story:
In 2009 a priest named Nicola Corradi was accused of abusing pupils at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona, and in 2011 the diocese flagged him. By then he was working at the same religious order's school in Mendoza, Argentina. Argentine police arrested him in 2016, and in 2019 an Argentine court sentenced him to 42 years for abusing deaf children there. The detail that matters is whose court it was: the conduct began in Italy and the finding was made on another continent.

Italy works in the other direction too, as somewhere to wait. Joseph Henn, a priest indicted in Arizona in 2003, moved to Italy and stayed free until his arrest in Rome in May 2019, although his extradition had been approved. Extradition is a government's agreement to hand a person over, and agreeing is not the same as going to fetch him.

Behind both is a gap. Italy has never held a national inquiry into abuse in church or state institutions, and "there are no official statistics". In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said that under the Lateran concordat, the treaty that governs relations between Italy and the Vatican, its priests have no obligation to report suspected abuse to the police. A complaint made to a bishop therefore stops with the bishop, and only the families who go to a police station themselves put anything into the public record. The survivors' group Rete l'Abuso has asked for years for an inquiry run from outside the church.

Italy's other roles are as a buyer and a destination. It took in 383 children from South Korea between 1965 and 2008, a programme in which a 2025 South Korean truth commission found state-enabled fraud, and 39 children from Romania in 2002, two years before Romania banned foreign adoption. Some of the children disappeared by El Salvador's armed forces during its civil war were adopted to Italy. It is the main arrival point for women and girls moved from Edo State in Nigeria through Niger and Libya, and a 2006 study on the Kenyan coast found Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of the clients of children being exploited there.

An empty national record is not evidence that little happened; here it is the predictable result of a rule that priests need not tell the police, and of nobody being appointed to count. When a country has no inquiry, ask who has the power to order one, and what the delay is worth to the institution that would be examined.

CHE.mechanism: Harm done to children by officials acting lawfully and on paper, which is why the Swiss record is so complete and why the only safeguard that failed was a signature nobody checked.
CHE.story:
In 1926 the Swiss foundation Pro Juventute started a programme it called the Charity for the Children of the Country Road. Until 1973 it took about 600 Yenish children from their families, members of a travelling community, and placed them in homes and with foster families; about 2,000 children of the Swiss Traveller community are thought to have been affected by such measures in all. The foundation was not acting against the state. Officials at every level of government shared staff with it and helped pay for it, which is how a private charity came to exercise a public power. On 20 February 2025 the Swiss government accepted a legal opinion that this persecution amounted to a crime against humanity under today's international law, though not to cultural genocide, and repeated its apology.

Those children were part of something larger. Between about 1930 and 1981, Swiss cantons and towns placed more than 60,000 people in roughly 650 institutions without a court order, meaning on an administrative decision: an official's signature, with no hearing and nothing to appeal against. Some children were sent to farms as indentured labourers, the Verdingkinder. An independent expert commission reported in September 2019 that people held this way were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. The government apologised in 2010, and a 2016 law created a "solidarity contribution" of 25,000 Swiss francs for victims of these compulsory measures: one fixed sum for everyone who qualified, rather than an amount argued case by case.

Switzerland also brought children in, and the paperwork failed in the same way. It received 1,111 South Korean children between 1968 and 1997. From the 1970s to 2000 Swiss authorities approved adoptions from Sri Lanka, India and Tibet of children often wrongly described as orphans, deciding on incomplete or falsified documents and making insufficient checks on the receiving families. In Sri Lanka in the 1980s babies were bought or taken from hospitals and paid women posed in court as the birth mothers, so the file a Swiss official read was a fiction assembled for him. The Federal Council admitted those failings in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended banning intercountry adoption altogether.

What the Swiss cases teach is that the worst outcomes for children here were not hidden; they were authorised, filed and funded, and were lawful when they happened. When you read about a placement or an adoption, ask whose signature approved it and whether that person ever verified the document in front of them.

ZAF.mechanism: A country that inherits men other institutions removed quietly, because a dismissal with a good reference and no police report sends an abuser abroad with a clean local record.
ZAF.story:
Fettes College in Edinburgh dismissed a teacher called Iain Wares in 1979 and gave him a glowing testimonial. He moved to South Africa, taught there, and abused children. A reference is the only thing most employers see, so a school that dismisses a man and praises him on paper has not removed a risk, it has relocated it. South Africa approved his extradition to Scotland, and he was still contesting that in 2025, nearly half a century after the dismissal.

Two other men arrived the same way. Georg Kerkhoff, a German priest with abuse cases pending at home, worked for years in South Africa and was tried there over the abuse of boys at a camp in 2008, then sent back and jailed in Krefeld in 2015. John Smyth QC, a barrister who had beaten boys at English evangelical camps and whose conduct an internal church report described in 1982, ran camps for boys in Zimbabwe, was refused re-entry there, and came to South Africa in 2001. He attended churches in Durban and then Cape Town, at one of them from 2004 to 2016, and the 2024 Makin review in England found it highly likely that he went on abusing until he died in Cape Town in 2018. He was never charged anywhere. In each case the South African congregation or school met a man with no local record, because the information had stayed in the country he left.

Cases that start inside the country run into a different problem: time. The pastor Timothy Omotoso was reported in 2017 and acted on in the same year, but applications for a mistrial and judges standing down stretched the proceedings over eight years. Pamela Mabini, a whistleblower in the case, was shot dead on 7 March 2025, weeks before the verdict. Delay is not neutral; it is an outcome someone can work towards.

The 2025 US trafficking report describes children recruited from rural areas and exploited in cities, especially Gauteng and the Western Cape, with brothel owners using drugs to keep control of them and some parents selling their own children for sex or for online abuse. It records low-level official corruption as persistent. South Africa sent 3,716 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022.

South Africa shows the receiving end of a transfer, which is where the cost of a quiet dismissal is actually paid, by children who had no way of knowing what the previous employer knew. When an institution removes someone over children, ask two things: what the next employer was told, and whether the police were told anything at all.

BGR.mechanism: Two unrelated roles that both make a country look responsible for something it is not doing itself: children parked in state institutions that nobody watches, and rented servers holding a quarter of the world's reported abuse material for customers who live elsewhere.
BGR.story:
A British documentary maker, Kate Blewett, filmed inside the state home at Mogilino and broadcast "Bulgaria's Abandoned Children" in 2007. It showed disabled children neglected there. In February 2008 Bulgaria's social affairs minister repeated a promise to close Mogilino and six similar homes, and children were being moved out by June. No sexual-abuse finding about Mogilino was located; this is a record of neglect. What makes it relevant is the scale behind it. Bulgaria has had one of the highest numbers of children living in state institutions in the European Union, and the 2025 US trafficking report cites a UN special rapporteur who found sexual exploitation, including possible trafficking, to be prevalent among children in government-run homes. A child in a large institution may have nobody who notices an absence for an evening.

The courts take the pressure off the other end. The same report counts 31 traffickers convicted, of whom only eight were sent to prison, and 34 convicted traffickers given suspended sentences, which means a conviction is recorded and no one goes to jail. It describes corruption in the police and the judiciary as pervasive. For anyone selling a child, that is a known and survivable cost.

Bulgaria's other role is as a landlord. The Internet Watch Foundation is a British charity that finds abuse material online and asks whoever hosts it to take it down. In 2025 it acted on 87,959 web addresses hosted in Bulgaria, 28 per cent of its worldwide total and up from 9 per cent the year before, and said the rise came from "just a few particular sites". Hosting means the files sit on rented computers in a data centre; the company renting them decides how quickly to respond, while the people uploading and paying can be anywhere in the world. The figure measures Bulgaria's hosting industry, not Bulgarian offenders.

The same infrastructure cuts the other way. In Operation Blackwrist, Bulgaria's cybercrime police took down the servers of a subscription site that published the abuse of boys in Thailand weekly to nearly 63,000 users; its administrator in Thailand was sentenced to 146 years and the one in Australia to 40 years and three months. Bulgaria sent 5,067 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, and that route is still open.

Bulgaria is the clearest case on this map of a country whose numbers are about where things are stored rather than where they are done. When you see a country named as the top host of abuse material, ask who owns the servers and how fast they answer a removal notice, and keep that question separate from who is abusing children there.

NPL.mechanism: Recruitment by promise rather than force, with a payment at every handover: school for a child whose parents are alive, a job or a marriage for a girl crossing an unmanned border.
NPL.story:
In the Karnali region of western Nepal, agents call on families and offer to put a child into school in the capital. The family pays. The child is delivered to a children's home in Kathmandu, which pays the agent a commission. Charities documented one child admitted on a forged certificate saying a parent had died, and UNICEF estimates that about 85 per cent of children in Nepal's registered homes have a living parent or guardian. The reason a home will pay for a child is that children attract donors and foreign visitors, so being an orphan is a document the institution needs rather than a fact about the child.

Those homes fed adoption abroad. In March 2007 a Daily Telegraph investigation described babies being bought, bribes paid and birth families deceived. A month later Nepal's new minister stopped all intercountry adoption, leaving about 400 Western families waiting; around 440 pending cases were processed from November 2007 and new rules were published in May 2008. The United States later suspended adoptions of Nepali children declared abandoned, because that declaration — the paper that says no parent can be found — could not be relied on. Nepal sent 1,991 children abroad between 2003 and 2022.

The larger movement runs south. The border with India is 1,850 kilometres long and open, with no checks to pass, and researchers estimate that 5,000 to 10,000 Nepali women and girls are taken across it each year to brothels in Kolkata, in Mumbai's Kamathipura district and elsewhere. The recruitment is an offer: a job, a marriage, or a romance that begins online. The 2025 US trafficking report says Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers in the year, 231 of them for sex trafficking, and cites a 2024 study finding that most workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were sex-trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. It also reports traffickers bribing some Indian officials to fly Nepali workers on to third countries. Offenders arrive as well: a Canadian aid worker who worked with street children abused boys at his home in Nepal.

Nepal shows that the first step is usually an agreement a parent or a young woman enters willingly, on information that is false, and that money changes hands at each handover. South Asia has no representative survey of online abuse, so there is no comparable measure of what happens through phones. When you read about a children's home here, ask how many of its children have living parents, who brought them, and who was paid for the delivery.

BIH.mechanism: Immunity as it actually works: the same country produced long sentences from an international court for its own soldiers and nothing at all for the foreign police and contractors, who were put on planes instead of in a dock.
BIH.story:
In Serb-held Foča in 1992, Bosniak women and girls were held in places like the Partizan Sports Hall, which stood next to the municipal police building, and taken from there to flats and houses to be raped. The UN set up a war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia so that these crimes could be tried outside the courts of the states involved. It found that Bosnian Serb forces used rape as an instrument of terror and that the local police guarded the women and took part in their mistreatment. In February 2001 it sentenced Dragoljub Kunarac to 28 years for torture, rape and enslavement; Radomir Kovač to 20 years, which included holding two girls in his flat for about four months and selling victims to other soldiers; and Zoran Vuković to 12 years, including the rape of a girl he knew to be 15. The sentences were upheld in 2002.

The peace brought a second market. From 1995 international police monitors, foreign officers sent to supervise the local force, and soldiers and civilian contractors arrived in numbers. Human Rights Watch reported in 2002 that women and girls, mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine, were sold to Bosnian bar owners and held by debts they were told they had to work off. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and customers. Eighteen UN police monitors who bought women, used brothels or faced trafficking-related charges were sent home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army investigation documented contractors for the American firm DynCorp buying women; one confessed to buying a woman for 1,600 Deutschmarks.

Sending a man home was not a soft punishment, it was the only one available, because foreign monitors and contractors could not be tried in Bosnian courts and their own governments did not take the cases up. Repatriation also removed them as witnesses against the bar owners. DynCorp dismissed one of its monitors, Kathryn Bolkovac, in April 2001 after she reported the trafficking; in August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found the dismissal unfair.

Bosnia sets the two outcomes side by side. Where a court with authority over the accused existed, the result was decades in prison; where it did not, the result was a flight home and a vacancy to fill. When peacekeepers, monitors or contractors are accused anywhere, ask which court has power over that person, and whether it ever sat.

MAR.mechanism: A finished conviction cancelled by an executive signature given for diplomatic reasons, with nobody reading the file to see whose sentence was being wiped out.
MAR.story:
Moroccan police arrested Daniel Galván, a retired Spanish professor, in December 2010. In September 2011 a court sentenced him to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged between 4 and 14. On 30 July 2013 King Mohammed VI pardoned 48 Spanish prisoners as a gesture to Spain, and Galván was on the list. A royal pardon is a decision by the head of state that cancels a sentence; no court reviews it and the victims are not heard. Galván left the country on an expired passport, with the authorities' knowledge.

People gathered outside parliament in Rabat to protest and were violently dispersed. On 4 August the king revoked the pardon, citing the gravity of the crimes and the rights of the victims, and said he had not been told the details of the case. That explanation is the mechanism in one line: a list of names had been approved as a favour between two governments without anyone checking what each man had been convicted of. Galván was by then in Spain, where he was arrested and imprisoned to serve out his sentence.

It was not the first time. A 2010 US diplomatic cable reported that in 2006 the king pardoned Hervé Le Gloannec, a Frenchman convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh, who was released.

Foreign offenders still arrive as tourists. The 2025 US trafficking report says charities find children exploited in Tangier inside holiday rentals owned and managed by Europeans, which matters because a rented flat has no reception desk, no register of guests and no staff who might notice a child being brought in. Morocco also sends soldiers out: Moroccan military personnel are named in the UN's tables of sexual exploitation and abuse allegations in the peacekeeping missions in the Central African Republic and DR Congo, where troops can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. The Middle East and North Africa has no representative survey of online abuse either, so there is no national measure to set against single cases like these.

Morocco shows that the last stage of a case is not the verdict. A sentence is held by the state, not by the children it was imposed for, and a state can trade it away. When a pardon, an amnesty or a prisoner transfer is presented as diplomacy, ask who is on the list and who read the convictions before it was signed.

SRB.mechanism: Institutions that hold disabled children behind a door outsiders cannot open, so the only account of what happens inside comes from a visiting group that was asked to leave, and no official count has followed it.
SRB.story:
For four years a group called Mental Disability Rights International visited Serbia's state institutions for people with mental disabilities, which between them held more than 17,000 people. Its report, released on 14 November 2007, described children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, filthy rooms, contagious disease and no outside oversight, treatment it called "tantamount to torture". On sexual abuse it reported a risk rather than a finding, and the reason is worth following. At the institution in Vršac, men and women lived in mixed wards and staff told the visitors that they made no effort to establish whether sex between residents was consensual. Nobody inside the building was asking the question that would identify a rape, so there was nothing for an inspector to find later.

The closing of the door was literal. In 2006 the director of one institution refused to let the visitors into a locked area and asked them to leave. Serbian officials called the allegations "dark propaganda", which is a cheap answer to a report but an effective one, because the group had no power to compel anything and no Serbian body took the findings over.

Serbia was also a transit country. After NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in Kosovo in 1999, Amnesty International reported in 2004 that Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution, brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia through Serbia, with local girls abducted as well. Amnesty put the international presence at 80 per cent of traffickers' income at the time, and found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries. The UN's peacekeeping department accepted in 2004 that peacekeepers had "come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution".

Serbia also appears among the countries connected to Nazi Germany's seizure of children judged racially valuable, who were given new identities with German families; a US military tribunal at Nuremberg convicted 13 of the 14 officials tried for it in 1948.

There is no case here in which a Serbian court or inquiry found sexual abuse of children inside a Serbian institution, and that absence is the point: the 2007 account came from outside, was rejected, and was never replaced by an official count. When a report on an institution is dismissed as propaganda, ask who has the legal right to walk in unannounced, and whether anyone has used it since.

BDI.mechanism: A troop-sending country: the UN can gather the accounts, identify the soldiers and fly them home, but only Burundi can charge them, and the file stops there.
BDI.story:
In 2016 UN investigators went to Dékoa, a town in the Central African Republic, to look into two allegations against peacekeepers from Burundi and Gabon. They interviewed some 136 alleged victims — 48 per cent of all the victims the UN recorded worldwide that year, from one town. Press accounts said at least 98 girls described abuse and that 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without charges. The UN's own tables list allegations against Burundian contingent personnel involving 46 children. The reason the trail ends there is a rule with no exceptions: soldiers lent to a UN mission remain subject only to the criminal law of the country that sent them. The Secretary-General's 2017 report recorded the two countries' investigations as still pending.

Burundian soldiers had been named earlier in Somalia. Human Rights Watch, after 50 interviews including 21 survivors, reported in September 2014 on abuse by African Union forces in Mogadishu: ten incidents of rape and sexual assault and 14 cases of sexual exploitation, mostly by Ugandan personnel at the mission's headquarters and by Burundian personnel at their own base. Four of the rape cases and one assault involved girls under 18, the youngest a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013. Many of the women and girls had come to the bases to ask for medicine or aid, one of them for a sick baby, and interpreters helped soldiers reach them. Some were pushed into sex in exchange for money, food or medicine. Where the base holds the only supply of help, the people guarding it set the price.

Inside Burundi itself, almost nothing reaches the international systems. In 2025 the US clearinghouse that receives reports of online child abuse from technology companies logged 1,028 reports connected to Burundi. That figure counts what American platforms noticed and forwarded, so it measures how much the country uses those platforms at least as much as it measures abuse there.

Burundi sits on this map mainly as a home country, which is the quiet half of every peacekeeping scandal: the accounts are taken abroad and the decision to prosecute is taken at home, by a government whose soldiers earn and whose reputation is at stake. When a contingent is sent home, ask whether a court in that country ever opened a case, and what has happened to it since.

AUT.mechanism: A city department that both ran a children's home and was meant to supervise it, and a church compensation scheme written by the institution the claims were against.
AUT.story:
The City of Vienna ran a children's home at Wilhelminenberg from 1948 to 1977, and from 1962 it took only girls. A complaint reached officials as early as 1960. The finding came 53 years later, in a 344-page report that a commission set up by the city presented in June 2013, built on 217 interviews, 140 of them with former residents. It found the girls were abused on a wide scale, including rape and sexual exploitation by the staff who cared for them and by men brought in from outside, with victims as young as about six. Staff in the municipal department that oversaw the home knew about it and did not act, and city politicians told in the 1960s ignored it. That is the ordinary shape of this failure: the body that ran the home was also the body expected to inspect it, so a complaint travelled to the people with the most to lose from it. The findings were sent to prosecutors, and some former residents were paid up to 35,000 euros.

The church's reckoning started three years earlier and on different terms. In spring 2010 Austria's bishops set up an independent commission for victims, known after its chair as the Klasnic Commission, which fixed compensation at four levels: 5,000 euros, 15,000, 25,000, and more in extreme cases. A commission appointed by the institution facing the claims cannot compel anyone to hand over a document or give evidence, and a scheme of fixed tiers means the institution decides in advance what a childhood is worth and keeps its total bill predictable. Payment and a public finding are not the same thing, and only one of them was on offer.

Austria is also a destination. The 2025 US trafficking report names it among the countries where Romanian women and girls are exploited, and says children in Romania's government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for people with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking.

Vienna shows how long a complaint can sit when the recipient is also the owner, and how differently a case ends depending on who sets the rules for admitting it. When a compensation scheme is announced, ask who chose the amounts, who decides which cases qualify, and whether anything a claimant says will ever be published as a finding.

MLI.mechanism: A war record made only of cases an investigator could reach and confirm, in which the national army appears on the same list as the groups it is fighting.
MLI.story:
The UN keeps a yearly count of attacks on children in Mali, and the word it uses for the ones it publishes is "verified": a case is counted only when UN staff have corroborated it themselves. In 2024 it verified the rape of 32 girls. In 22 of those cases the perpetrators could not be identified, which usually means the child could describe what was done but not by whom, because the men were armed and in no recognisable uniform. Four cases were attributed to the Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, three to the al-Qaeda-linked group JNIM, two to Mali's own armed forces and one to the militia Ganda Lassal Izo. The UN also verified the abduction of 119 children, four of them by foreign security personnel working in the country. In 2023 it had verified the rape of 15 girls, four of them by Mali's army.

Verification sets the floor, not the total. Investigators have to travel to the child, the child has to be alive and willing to speak, and someone has to be able to corroborate it, so the published figure is bounded by where UN staff can safely go. In a conflict spread across a very large country, the gap between the count and the reality is unknown and is not estimated.

The presence of Mali's army on the list creates the second problem. Soldiers are prosecuted by their own state, and here the state that would have to bring the charges is the state whose troops are named in the finding.

Mali is also a destination. The 2025 US trafficking report says organised Nigerian networks, some tied to cult groups, move Nigerian women and girls into prostitution in the gold-mining regions of Mali, Senegal, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire — places where men work for cash far from home, which is the usual market this trade follows. West and Central Africa has no representative survey of online abuse.

What Mali teaches is how to read a UN number: it is a count of confirmations, not of events, and it names whoever investigators could identify, which is why so many entries say nobody. When you next see an annual figure from a war, ask who verified it, where they were unable to travel, and whether the government in question appears among the accused.

MDG.mechanism: A destination that filled up when the neighbouring country tightened its law, and a trade that has since stopped needing the traveller at all.
MDG.story:
When Mozambique tightened its laws against child sex tourism, observers recorded the trade growing in Madagascar instead, with offenders mostly French and Italian. That is the whole logic of a travelling offender: he chooses a country the way a tourist chooses a beach, and weak enforcement is one of the attractions, so tougher law in one place is often a transfer rather than a reduction.

What he arrives into is mostly local. The 2025 US trafficking report says most children sold for sex in Madagascar are exploited by Malagasy men, with foreign tourists, often French, exploiting children as well. Some parents encourage daughters into paid sex with tourists, and children are exploited in karaoke bars in the capital, Antananarivo. The foreign demand sits on top of an existing market rather than creating one, which is why closing a bar or deporting a visitor changes little.

Then the journey became unnecessary. In July 2025 police on the tourist island of Nosy Be arrested two women suspected of filming the abuse of their own children and selling the videos to foreign buyers, who paid by mobile phone money transfer; they were charged. A buyer like that needs no visa, no flight and no hotel, and cannot be caught at a border. The money reaches the household directly, so the person being paid is the person the child lives with.

Enforcement in Madagascar is thin. Courts convicted 15 traffickers in the year the US report covers, and those were the first convictions in four years, meaning the offence existed in law throughout that period without producing a case. The report calls corruption and official complicity significant concerns and says one official was investigated. Nosy Be has its own anti-trafficking committee.

Madagascar is where you can see that a crackdown measured by local numbers can be a success and a failure at once: offenders left Mozambique, arrived here, and then found they did not have to arrive anywhere. When one country's figures fall, ask which country's rose, and whether the trade has simply moved from a hotel room to a phone.

HUN.mechanism: A conviction for concealing abuse erased by an unannounced presidential pardon, which came to light only because a reporter went looking a year later.
HUN.story:
In 2022 a Hungarian court sentenced Endre Kónya, the former deputy director of the children's home in Bicske, to three years and four months. His offence was not abuse but helping the home's director cover up the director's sexual abuse of children. Concealment is punished separately because it is what keeps a man in post: as long as nobody outside the building knows, the children stay where they are.

In April 2023, ahead of a visit by the Pope, President Katalin Novák pardoned about two dozen people, and Kónya was one of them. A pardon cancels a sentence without any court being involved. Hungary requires a minister to countersign, which is meant to be a check on exactly this kind of decision, and the justice minister, Judit Varga, signed. Nothing was announced.

The pardon surfaced on 2 February 2024, when the news site Telex reported it, nearly a year after it was granted. Protests followed. On 10 February Novák resigned, saying she had made a mistake, and Varga announced the same day that she was leaving public life. Prime Minister Viktor Orbán then proposed amending the constitution so that nobody convicted of a crime against children could be pardoned, which is an admission that the existing procedure had allowed it.

Hungary also sends children abroad for adoption: 2,868 between 2003 and 2022, and the route remains open.

The Bicske case shows that the end of a prosecution is not always the end of the story, and that the most powerful office in a country can undo a sentence without publishing the fact. When you read that someone was convicted of covering up abuse, ask whether pardons in that country are published as a matter of course, and who is responsible for reading each file before it is signed.

PSE.mechanism: A war in which the only established record is what one UN commission was able to find, and what it found included boys as deliberate targets.
PSE.story:
In June 2024 a UN commission of inquiry reported on the war that began in October 2023. A commission of inquiry is a body the UN Human Rights Council appoints to establish facts; it cannot arrest anyone or compel a government, and what it records depends on the access and the testimony it can obtain. This one covered the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel.

It found that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence, including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, during arrests and in detention, and that "men and boys were targeted in particular ways". It found the persecution of Palestinian men and boys on the basis of gender to be a crime against humanity. That phrase has a specific meaning: treating a group badly because of their sex, as part of a wider attack on a population, which is a charge an international court can act on rather than a description of individual cruelty.

The same commission found that sexual violence was committed during the attacks of 7 October 2023 at the Nova music festival, at Nahal Oz and at several kibbutzim, and that 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage.

Beyond those findings there is nothing here to count. This map records the war only to the extent of what the commission established; there are no case-by-case tallies of abuse of Palestinian children, and the Middle East and North Africa has no representative survey of online abuse to draw on either. In a war, the only counters are the bodies that can reach witnesses, and when those bodies are few, the record is as small as their reach.

What this entry teaches is to read a wartime finding carefully: who investigated, what access they had, and the exact words they used, because "found" and "alleged" are different things and the commission used both. It also corrects a common assumption, since it found boys were targeted in particular ways, not only girls.

VIR.mechanism: A case pursued through the money rather than the man, which produced very large payments, regulatory bans and not one criminal finding.
VIR.story:
Jeffrey Epstein owned Little St. James, a private island in the US Virgin Islands. Lawsuits describe a sex-trafficking operation run partly from it between 1998 and 2019, with girls brought from the US mainland. A private island is a useful instrument for this: the owner decides who flies in, who crews the boats and who is allowed to leave, and there are no neighbours.

After Epstein's death the territory's government went after the money instead. It reached a settlement of $105m with his estate and $62.5m with the billionaire Leon Black. In December 2022 it sued JPMorgan Chase, which had been Epstein's bank, arguing that the bank ignored warning signs and assisted him by keeping him as a client. In June 2023 JPMorgan agreed to pay $290m to nearly 200 of Epstein's victims in a class action, and in September 2023 to pay the Virgin Islands $75m. Earlier, in July 2020, New York's financial regulator fined Deutsche Bank $150m for ignoring red flags about him, and British regulators permanently banned a former JPMorgan banker, Jes Staley, for recklessly misleading them about his relationship with Epstein, a ban upheld in June 2025.

Every one of those outcomes is a civil settlement or a regulatory penalty. A settlement is a payment agreed to end a lawsuit; it records no admission, establishes no facts and usually leaves the evidence untested in public. So the money moved and nobody was convicted, which is why suing a bank is both the most effective route available here and an incomplete one.

The reason the route worked at all is that banks keep records. A trafficking operation has to pay for flights, staff, property and silence, and those payments pass through institutions that are legally required to notice unusual activity and report it.

The Virgin Islands entry shows how to follow this kind of case when the central figure is dead or untouchable: look at who handled the money and what they were told. When a wealthy person is accused, ask which banks kept the account open, what warnings they had on file, and whether the result was a verdict or a cheque.

TUR.mechanism: A marriage performed outside the state's registry, which leaves no document naming the girl and therefore nothing for an official to notice.
TUR.story:
Türkiye has hosted about 2.9 million Syrians displaced by the war across its border. The 2025 US trafficking report says that among them, Syrian girls are married off in unofficial religious ceremonies, particularly in poor rural regions, and are then subjected to domestic servitude and sex trafficking. Families and brokers arrange the ceremonies.

The word that carries the weight there is unofficial. A registered marriage creates a record with a date and two names on it, and an age that a clerk, a school or a doctor can question. A ceremony that is never registered creates nothing. The girl does not appear as a wife, so there is no entry anyone can check against her age, and if she stops going to school nobody is obliged to ask where she went. For the family receiving money and the broker arranging it, the absence of paperwork is the point, not an oversight.

The same report says Türkiye reported no investigations of officials involved in trafficking during the year, while describing corruption and complicity as significant concerns. Those two statements sit together: the concern is on the record, and no investigation was reported that could have tested it.

Türkiye has been a destination for longer than the Syrian war. In March 2007 the US State Department reported that women and children from Moldova were being trafficked for sexual exploitation, increasingly to Russia and the Middle East, including Türkiye, Israel and the United Arab Emirates. UNICEF found that children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more likely to be trafficked than other children, because a child who ages out of an institution has no family to return to and no one who expects a phone call.

The lesson here is about documents. A child can be sold inside a ceremony the state does not record, and no national statistic will ever show her. When you read that refugee girls are being married, ask who registers marriages in that country, what happens if nobody does, and which official is supposed to notice a 14-year-old who has left school.

SAU.mechanism: A country that exists on this map only inside other countries' reports: children arriving in it are counted by the country they came from, and men leaving it are counted by the country they travel to.
SAU.story:
Saudi Arabia has no case of its own here. It appears twice, and both times in a document written about somewhere else. The 2025 US trafficking report's chapter on Ethiopia says organised begging rings exploit Ethiopian women and children in Saudi Arabia. Its chapter on Indonesia says Middle Eastern tourists pay for short "contract marriages" with girls as young as nine in Puncak, in West Java. One entry describes children brought in; the other describes demand going out.

That is a pattern worth recognising rather than a coincidence. These reports are compiled country by country, and each chapter is built from what that government, its police and local organisations will supply. A country that does not publish its own data on the subject can still show up in a neighbour's chapter, because the neighbour is counting its own departing citizens. So the record of Saudi Arabia on this map is assembled from the outside, by people watching the exits and entrances.

What happens to children inside the country is not measured in these sources at all. Childlight, a research centre that pools surveys of child sexual abuse to build global estimates, reported in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation; its figures rest on surveys from only 60 countries.

A "contract marriage" of the kind described in Puncak also deserves a plain explanation: a ceremony gives the transaction a name a hotel can accept and a border official is unlikely to query, which is what paying for a child is called when it needs to look lawful.

The blank space over Saudi Arabia is a record of who is doing the counting, not of what is happening. Before treating any country's figures as comparable, ask what it would have to publish — a victim count, court outcomes, a survey of its own children — for a comparison to mean anything.

DJI.mechanism: A transit country, where children are in motion and the only record of them is a sentence in the report about the country they left.
DJI.story:
Everything this map holds about Djibouti comes from a chapter about Ethiopia. The 2025 US trafficking report says Ethiopian girls are exploited in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in Djibouti and in Sudan. Djibouti lies on the route from Ethiopia towards the Red Sea and the Arabian Peninsula, and that position explains both the case and the silence around it.

A child who is moving is hard to count. She is registered nowhere she passes through, she is in the country for weeks or months rather than years, and she is often inside a private house as a domestic worker, which is the least visible workplace there is. There is no employer's register to inspect, no school roll she drops off, and no agency that was ever told she arrived. If she is counted at all, it is by someone studying where she came from, which is why the entry appears under Ethiopia's name and not Djibouti's.

The region also has no measurement of abuse online. Childlight, a research centre that pools surveys to produce global estimates, found in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa lack representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation; its estimates draw on surveys from only 60 countries. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 of them supplied data for 2023, so even the best international count is built mainly from the governments that chose to answer.

Djibouti teaches that the map's gaps often follow movement: countries people travel through produce the least data about them, because being counted usually requires staying put. When a route is described, ask who keeps a record at each stop along it, and whether anyone counts a child who crosses a border with no papers at all.

LVA.mechanism: An adoption route shut by law with no published reason, which shows how often the decision to stop sending children abroad is made without any finding being released.
LVA.story:
On 1 July 2022 a Latvian law took effect that prevents the adoption of Latvian children to the United States. The source for this is the US government's own adoption report for 2024, which records the law as a fact of the system it has to administer. Nothing in the material behind this map explains what prompted it, and nothing is invented here to fill the space.

The absence is itself informative, because it is normal. Intercountry adoption has moved from one sending country to the next as each was examined: Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2007 and 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal, and Ethiopia, which banned foreign adoption in 2018. In those cases inquiries found children who had been bought, taken or registered as orphans while a parent was alive, and the route closed afterwards. But a closure and a published finding are two separate acts, and governments frequently do the first without the second. A law can be passed because of a specific scandal, because of a change in policy about children in care, or because officials no longer trust the paperwork, and the text of the law will often say none of this.

That leaves two different questions, and they need to be kept apart. One is what the country found, if anything. The other is what happened to the children sent abroad before the route closed, which nobody is obliged to go back and check: once an adoption is finalised the child is a citizen of the receiving country, and the sending country's file is closed.

Latvia is a useful reminder not to read a closed route as proof of wrongdoing, or an open one as proof that nothing is wrong. When a country stops sending children abroad, ask what it found and whether it ever said so, and ask separately who followed up on the children who had already gone.

RWA.mechanism: A receiving country deciding to stop taking children from a sending country, which closes the route without anyone having to explain what was wrong with it.
RWA.story:
The single entry for Rwanda on this map was made in Dublin. On 10 October 2007 Ireland's Adoption Board suspended adoptions from Ethiopia and Rwanda. The material behind this map does not record the reason, and none is supplied here.

The direction of that decision is the thing to notice. In intercountry adoption, the receiving country holds the switch. It can refuse to issue visas or recognise placements, and when it does so the route closes whatever the sending country's own view is. A board in one capital can therefore write the only line in the record about a country thousands of kilometres away, and it is under no obligation to publish what persuaded it — a pattern of documents it did not believe, a warning from another government, or a case it would rather not discuss.

The wider sequence gives the context. Intercountry adoption shifted from one sending country to the next as each was examined, Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2007 and 2008, then Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia, which banned foreign adoption outright in 2018. Each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or wrongly registered as orphans, and each closure moved the demand on rather than ending it: the families waiting did not stop wanting a child, so agencies looked for the next country with weak paperwork and many institutions.

Rwanda shows how thin a country's record can be and still be accurate: one suspension, by someone else, for undisclosed reasons. When a receiving country suspends adoptions from somewhere, ask what its board had in front of it, whether that material was ever published, and which country the agencies turned to next.

GNB.mechanism: A country that has never been surveyed, which is the only instrument that can find abuse nobody reported — so its place on the map is set by the absence of a questionnaire rather than by anything about its children.
GNB.story:
There is one tool that can measure child sexual abuse in a country, and Guinea-Bissau has never had it used on it. A representative survey asks several thousand people, chosen so that they stand in for the population as a whole, what happened to them as children. It finds the abuse that was never reported to anyone, which is most of it, and it produces a rate that can be compared with another country's rate. Everything else — police files, court records, charity caseloads — counts only the people who came forward and were believed.

Childlight, a research centre that pools these surveys into global estimates, reported in its 2026 update that West and Central Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation. Its worldwide figures rest on surveys from 60 countries in total. Guinea-Bissau is not one of them, and so it contributes nothing to the number the world uses.

A survey of this kind is expensive and intrusive. Someone has to pay for interviewers, train them to ask children and adults about sexual abuse without causing harm, obtain a government's permission, and then accept publishing a number that will be reported as a national embarrassment. Each of those is a reason a survey does not happen, and none of them has anything to do with how safe children are.

So Guinea-Bissau has no case on this map, and that is a fact about research budgets and political will. A country with no data is a question, not an answer. When you see an empty space on a map like this one, ask whether anyone has ever surveyed children there, who would have paid for it, and which government would have had to agree to the result being published.

KWT.mechanism: A country with no survey, where the only possible numbers are the ones its police record and its government chooses to release.
KWT.story:
When no survey exists, a country's figures on child sexual abuse can only come from its own institutions, and that limits them in a specific way. A police statistic counts reports: a child or a parent has to tell someone, an officer has to write it down, and the case has to be classified under the right heading. Anything that stops at any of those three steps never enters the number. The figure also belongs to the government, which decides what to compile, what to publish and whether to send it to anyone abroad.

Kuwait has no recorded case on this map, and no measurement behind it. Childlight, a research centre that pools population surveys into global estimates, reported in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation; its worldwide figures draw on surveys from only 60 countries. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023, which shows how much of even the main international count depends on a government filling in a form.

The practical result is that a reader has nothing to work with. There is no rate to compare, no conviction count to set against it, and no independent study to check either one. An absence of records cannot be read as an absence of harm, and it cannot be read as evidence of harm either; it simply means the question has not been asked by anyone whose answer reaches this map.

Kuwait is the case for treating a blank as a description of the measuring system. Before accepting any country's silence, ask whether a survey of children has ever been run there, whether the police publish what they record, and whether the government reports to the international systems that assemble the world totals.

IRN.mechanism: The arithmetic of the global figures: a country that does not report is simply left out, so the world total is not an estimate of the world but a sum of the countries that answered.
IRN.story:
The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries. Only 72 of them supplied data for 2023. The remaining entries rest on older figures or on none, and the total published is the sum of what arrived, not a measurement of the planet. Iran is among the countries that contribute nothing to it, and this map holds no recorded case of child abuse or trafficking inside the country.

It helps to see what that does to a number. If a country with tens of millions of children reports no cases, the global count does not rise by an estimate for it; it rises by zero. The country's absence therefore pushes the world figure down, and the published total reads as smaller and safer than the reality it is supposed to describe. The same applies to rates. Childlight, a research centre that pools population surveys into global estimates, reported in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation, and that its worldwide estimates rest on surveys from only 60 countries. A region that is not surveyed is quietly represented by the regions that were.

None of this is specific to Iran's conduct. Any state that does not run a survey, does not publish police data or does not answer an international questionnaire has the same effect, and a government has reasons to prefer that: a number once published can be compared, repeated and used against it.

Iran is the clearest illustration of how a world total is built and what it leaves out. When you are given a global figure for abused or trafficked children, ask how many countries reported, which ones did not, and whether anything at all was estimated in their place.

TGO.mechanism: A record that follows researchers rather than children: where studies have been funded and permitted, cases exist, and where they have not, a country stays blank.
TGO.story:
Every figure on this map exists because somebody paid for a count. That is the shortest explanation of why Togo has no recorded case of child sexual abuse or trafficking here. The record is thickest where people looked, and looking takes money, access and a government willing to let it happen.

Childlight, a research centre that pools population surveys into global estimates, reported in its 2026 update that West and Central Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation. Its global figures are built from surveys in 60 countries. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023. In 2025, 14 per cent of the 23.4 million reports to the US clearing house for online child abuse reports could not be attributed to any country at all.

Consider what it takes for a case to reach a map like this. A child has to tell someone; that person has to be in a job where reporting is expected; a police force has to record it under a category that is later counted; a court has to reach a verdict; and a journalist, an inquiry or an international agency has to publish it in a language and a format that someone compiling a global dataset will find. A country can fail at any one of those stages and appear to have no problem.

Togo is a reminder that this map is a picture of attention as much as of harm. When a country is blank, ask who has ever been funded to study children there, who would have had to grant them access, and what the published record would look like if the same effort had been spent there as in western Europe.

ERI.mechanism: A number so small that it measures the reporting pipeline instead of the country: 11 reports describe how little Eritrea touches the American platforms that do the reporting.
ERI.story:
In 2025 the US clearing house that receives reports of online child abuse logged 11 reports connected to Eritrea. The same year it received 23.4 million reports in total, and could not attribute 14 per cent of them to any country. North Korea accounted for 12.

Eleven is not a measurement of abuse in Eritrea. Almost all of these reports come from technology companies, which scan their own services for known abuse images and send what they find. A report therefore requires several things in sequence: someone in the country using an American platform, uploading or sharing material on it, the company's systems detecting it, and the resulting report carrying enough information — usually an internet address — to be tied to a place. Where few people use those services, almost nothing is generated, however much harm is occurring offline. The figure is a measure of a country's exposure to a particular reporting system.

This is why putting such numbers side by side is misleading. A country with cheap smartphones and widespread use of the big social apps will produce reports in their thousands; a country with little connectivity will produce a handful, and look safer for it. Eritrea also has no survey of its children behind that number, and no case recorded inside it on this map, so the 11 has nothing to be checked against.

Eritrea is the place to learn the habit of asking what a figure counts before deciding what it proves. A very small number can be as uninformative as no number at all, and in this one both the top and the bottom of the global table are shaped by who is online rather than by who is being harmed.
